# Code review {#code-review}

::: {.tada-key}
**Code review** means checking and evaluating each other's code, either
**formally**, as part of peer review, or **informally**, as co-authors or
colleagues. It helps catch **conceptual, programmatic and syntactic errors**, and
it can happen at any stage of the research cycle.
:::

This chapter follows [Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023)]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}, *Implementing code review in the
scientific workflow: Insights from ecology and evolutionary biology* (Journal of
Evolutionary Biology 36: 1347–1356, <https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230>).

## Why it is missing, and why it matters {#review-why}

You probably already use open-source software such as R or Python to clean,
manipulate, visualise and analyse your data. Code-based software is more
transparent, reproducible and flexible than point-and-click software, because
analyses can be tailored to what a study needs.

That flexibility has a cost. **Code is more error-prone**
([Budd et al. 1998]{.tada-cite data-key="budd-1998"}), and several high-profile
retractions have followed coding mistakes
([Bolnick & Paull 2009]{.tada-cite data-key="bolnick-2009"};
[Huijgen et al. 2012]{.tada-cite data-key="huijgen-2012"};
[Ma & Chang 2007]{.tada-cite data-key="ma-2007"};
[Miller 2006]{.tada-cite data-key="miller-2006"};
[Williams & Bürkner 2020]{.tada-cite data-key="williams-2020"}).

In computer science and software development, code review is routine. In the
academic disciplines that rely on code to make inferences and predictions, it is
**largely absent** from the research and publication process
([Indriasari et al. 2020]{.tada-cite data-key="indriasari-2020"}). We argue for a
shift in research culture that brings code review into **all stages** of the
research process ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}).

Part of the reason is structural. Informal training, together with too little
time and too few incentives
([Touchon & McCoy 2016]{.tada-cite data-key="touchon-2016"}), means coding and
analysis are often the responsibility of **a single member of a team** for the
whole project, unlike methodology and experimental design, which the whole team
usually develops. Because research code is so often one person's work,
pre-publication code review is unlikely to happen, and important when it does.

## The four Rs {#review-four-rs}

The core priorities are the same at every stage. We frame them as four
questions ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}).

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reported]{.tada-word}
[Does the code match the description of what is reported in the methods
section?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Run]{.tada-word}
[Can the code actually be executed?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reliable]{.tada-word}
[Does the code give the correct result, not just a result, on every
run?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .neutral}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reproducible]{.tada-word}
[Do the outputs match the results reported in the paper?]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

::: {.tabset}

### Reported {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code is a key research output and part of the scientific method. Open code to
accompany written methods is becoming more common, following similar pushes for
Open and FAIR data
([Lamprecht et al. 2020]{.tada-cite data-key="lamprecht-2020"}). The first
check is therefore **consistency between the code and the manuscript**, which
catches **conceptual** errors.

*Does the code match what the methods section says was done?* If the methods
describe a generalised linear model with Poisson error and the code fits a
Gaussian one, the review has to pick that up.

**Software and package versions.** At minimum, list the packages central to the
analysis or visualisation, with version numbers, somewhere in the manuscript. In
R you can get these with `citation()`; in Python, with `setuptools`. A full list
of everything used, including packages for cleaning and tidying, can go
elsewhere: the README, or the `session_info.txt` described in
[Documented](#documented-readme), is the natural place.

This is more than bookkeeping. If a package version is later found to contain a
bug, you can identify the papers that depend on it.

**Environment management** also helps. It is beyond TADA's minimum standard
(see [Beyond TADA](#transferable-beyond)), but worth using where you can.
Packages such as **`renv`**
([Ushey & Wickham 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ushey-2023"}), which replaces `packrat` ([Ushey et al. 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="ushey-2022"}), and
**`groundhog`** ([Simonsohn & Gruson 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="simonsohn-2023"}) in R, or **`poetry`** ([Eustace 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="eustace-2023"})
and **`pipenv`** ([Pipenv Maintainer Team 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="pipenv-2023"}) in Python, help make the
environment reproducible and let you load specific package versions.
Containerisation with **Docker** ([Boettiger 2015]{.tada-cite data-key="boettiger-2015"}) is another option.

### Run {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code that matches the methods in a paper does not necessarily run.
**Programmatic and syntactic errors** can stop it re-running.

Common causes are listed below. The first two are from our code review paper ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}) and the
rest from Stage 5 of the SORTEE guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}), which lists the same
failures from the data editor's side:

- calls to libraries or modules that are not installed in the current
  environment
- spelling mistakes
- local or absolute file paths that do not exist on the reviewer's machine
- missing files, or filenames in the code that do not match the archived files
- variable names in the code that do not match those in the data files
- a missing code chunk

This is the easiest of the four checks, yet it fails often: 74% of over 9,000
archived R files failed to complete without error ([Trisovic
et al. 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="trisovic-2022"}).

::: {.tada-tip}
Run it in a **fresh session**, from a **fresh download**, in a **new folder**.
Anything that only works because of what is already loaded in your environment
will fail, and that is what you are trying to find.
:::

### Reliable {.unlisted .unnumbered}

This is the hardest of the four checks, and it needs a reviewer who knows the
study.

Code can run perfectly well, produce an output and still be wrong, because
**code can produce incorrect results reproducibly**, giving the same wrong
answer every time. For example, if code selects or modifies the wrong column in
a dataset, the analysis is wrong but nothing errors ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}).

**Unit testing** helps, with **`testthat`** ([Wickham 2011]{.tada-cite data-key="wickham-2011"}) in R and
**`pytest`** ([Okken 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="okken-2022"}) in Python. But this type of error remains common and
is **extremely difficult to pick up without deep familiarity with the dataset
and code**. It is also thought to increase with the number of lines and the
complexity of the code ([Lipow 1982]{.tada-cite data-key="lipow-1982"}).

::: {.tada-note}
This is the strongest argument for **co-author** review over external review. A
reviewer who does not know your data cannot tell that `mass` should have been
`mass_g`. A co-author can.
:::

### Reproducible {.unlisted .unnumbered}

The basic question is whether **the code can produce the output, and so
support the conclusions, given in the paper**.

The final step of code review is to check that the outputs, when the code is
re-run, match those reported in the analysis and results sections, including
the relevant figures and the narrative text.

**When exact matching is not possible.** Apply some tolerance, especially with
stochastic methods, where parameter estimates change between runs, or with
computationally demanding and slow techniques. A mismatch happens, for example,
when `set.seed()` (R) or `random.seed()` (Python) was not used before stochastic
sampling.

Providing model outputs helps. Save them with `saveRDS()` in R or
`pickle.dump()` in Python, though a reviewer then cannot run the code themselves
to see whether they get similar results. Where the code cannot be re-run in
reasonable time, compare the newly generated results with those originally
reported.

The literature gives two criteria for judging a match.

*Conclusion and numbers* ([Archmiller et al. 2020]{.tada-cite data-key="archmiller-2020"}). Compare the **conclusion**,
meaning direction and significance level, and the **numbers**, meaning intervals
matching within one significant figure. Their worked example:

| Original | Reproduced | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 4.12, interval 3.45–4.91 | Conclusion **and** numbers reproduced |
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 6.5, interval 6.0–7.0 | Same conclusion; numbers **not** quantitatively reproduced |
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 4.10, interval −1.00–8.40 | **Not** reproduced, because the interval now overlaps zero |

*Percentage error* ([Hardwicke et al. 2021]{.tada-cite data-key="hardwicke-2021"}; see also [Kambouris et al. 2024]{.tada-cite data-key="kambouris-2024"}).
Comparison at one significant figure depends heavily on scale, whereas
percentage error does not. Using

$$\text{PE} = \frac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100$$

error is classified as **non-existent** when this value is 0, **minor** between
0 and 10, and **major (and not reproducible)** at 10 or above.

::: {.tada-wiki}
The formula as published is signed. In practice, it is the absolute value that
is compared against those thresholds.
:::

Whether the interval overlaps zero (or the null value) should be the same in
the reported and reproduced results, and the two sets of estimates and intervals
should not differ significantly from each other. With stochastic MCMC methods, variation between chains is
expected to be much lower than variation within a chain, so the reproduced value
should sit well within the reported credible interval.

:::

## Writing reviewable code {#review-reviewable}

Code review depends on readable code. We suggest four
solutions ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}):

1. **Call packages explicitly** via the namespace: `package::function()` in R,
   `package.module.function()` in Python.
2. **Use relative file paths**, for example the `here` package
   ([Müller & Bryan 2020]{.tada-cite data-key="muller-bryan-2020"}), preferably with an R project file if you use R and
   RStudio, or a virtual environment in Python.
3. **Remove redundant packages.**
4. **Write analysis code with clear subheadings, intuitive comments and
   easy-to-understand object names.**

For style, **`styler`** ([Müller & Walthert 2020]{.tada-cite data-key="muller-walthert-2020"}) reformats R code to a
standard style in one command, while **`pycodestyle`** ([Rocholl 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="rocholl-2022"}) checks
Python code against PEP 8, with `black`
([Python Software Foundation n.d.]{.tada-cite data-key="black"}) or `autopep8`
([autopep8 contributors n.d.]{.tada-cite data-key="autopep8"}) to do the
reformatting. Supported styles include Google and tidyverse in R, and PEP 8 in
Python.

Literate formats (R and Python Markdown, Quarto, and Jupyter Notebook or
JupyterLab) show code in chunks that, with descriptive comments, are much easier
to read. See [Annotated](#annotated-literate).

### Structure {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A simple folder and file structure helps researchers at any skill level follow
the **order and flow** of an analysis:

- **Sequentially labelled** subfolders and scripts, so someone following the
  code knows the order to run things in, with files beginning `01…`, `02…`
- **Folders named for their purpose**, such as `data`, `scripts` and `functions`
- **Raw data kept separate**, so cleaning or wrangling code cannot modify or
  overwrite it by accident
- A **README** and any other metadata a reader needs to re-run the code:
  packages and version numbers, descriptions of the data files, the project aim,
  author contact details and any licences

You should also **explain any data cleaning or curation that happened before the
analysis code**: what manipulation or pre-processing produced the data in its
current state, or where an intermediate data file was used.

::: {.tada-note}
**Metadata tooling.** Packages such as `codemeta` ([Boettiger 2017]{.tada-cite data-key="boettiger-2017"}) and
`dataReporter` ([Petersen & Ekstrøm 2019]{.tada-cite data-key="petersen-2019"}) in R, or `CodeMetaPy` ([van Gompel 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="van-gompel-2023"})
and `cookiecutter` ([Feldroy 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="feldroy-2022"}) in Python, can help produce consistent
metadata and project templates. Pipeline tools automate the steps from raw
data to results: `targets` ([Landau 2021]{.tada-cite data-key="landau-2021"}) and `workflowr`
([Blischak et al. 2019]{.tada-cite data-key="blischak-2019"}) in R, and `luigi` ([The Luigi Authors 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="luigi-authors-2023"}) in Python.
:::

## When code review happens {#review-when}

Code review can start when a project starts, and it is useful beyond
publication.

::: {.tabset}

### Pre-submission {.unlisted .unnumbered}

::: {.tada-wiki}
**This is where most of the value is.** It is also where a reviewer can catch
*Reliable* errors, because they know the study.
:::

Collaborate on code **continuously, at every stage** of a manuscript.
Platforms such as GitHub help, since users can submit and comment on pull
requests. At SORTEE, we used GitHub issues to summarise the discussion of an
individual's code.

The [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) give authors the same advice, under "Perform a pre-submission code review" ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}); see
[Advice for authors](#sharing-authors) for what that review should cover.

### During peer review {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Peer review is one of the most important places for code review, because
reviewers can follow the logic of the analyses much as they follow the argument
from introduction to discussion.

Some journals already request code and data at submission, including
[The Royal Society]{.tada-cite data-key="royal-society-2023"},
*[Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology]{.tada-cite data-key="bakker-2020"}* and
*[The American Naturalist]{.tada-cite data-key="bolnick-2022"}*, though in our
experience this is not enforced ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}). In some
cases, such as the **Journal of Open Source Software**, the entire formal
peer-review process, code and manuscript alike, is hosted on GitHub.

Both sides benefit
([Fernández-Juricic 2021]{.tada-cite data-key="fernandez-juricic-2021"}). For
authors, providing code during peer review could improve the manuscript. For
reviewers, available code gives much more insight, because the link between
experimental methods and statistical analysis is clearer. That is the first R,
code **as reported**.

There are two practical obstacles.

*Finding reviewers.* Willing reviewers are already in short supply. It is
reasonable to expect a reviewer to check that code is **as reported**, but
anything deeper takes time from overworked academics who may not have the right
expertise. A workable compromise is for reviewers to say whether they can check
that the code is as reported, and for the journal to make sure **at least one**
reviewer has checked the code.

*Double-blind review.* Anonymised data and code can be submitted directly to the
journal, for example as a zip file, or uploaded to Figshare, OSF, GitHub or
Dryad, which allow authors to provide an **anonymised link** for peer review.

### Post-publication {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Post-publication review is discussed much less. It cannot stop incorrect results
being published, but it does let you check the four Rs afterwards.

The first question is whether **all the code used to produce the results has been
made available**. If not, the main option is to ask the corresponding author or
the journal, much as data are requested "upon reasonable request".

**If you find that the code does not adhere to one of the Rs:**

1. **Contact the corresponding author**, or, if the paper uses the MeRIT system
   ([Nakagawa et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="nakagawa-2023"}), the person who conducted the analysis. A GitHub issue works well if
   there is a repository. Otherwise, email.
2. **Rule out harmless causes** first, such as differences in R or package
   versions, or the stochasticity inherent in simulations and MCMC sampling.
3. **Let the authors go to the journal themselves.** If there is a genuine
   error, the authors should get the chance to contact the journal and correct
   their own mistake.

::: {.tada-note}
Journal culture matters here. Under *The American Naturalist*'s stance
([Bolnick 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="bolnick-2022"}), authors who contact the journal to correct code or data errors
are **not penalised**, and corrections are encouraged where warranted. Where
updated results would change the narrative of a published paper, corrections are
harder, and publication versioning or "living" documents may be a first step
([Kane & Amin 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="kane-2023"}).
:::

:::

## Running a code club {#review-club}

A code club is a good way to set up peer code review within a lab or among
colleagues. This section draws on our experience building a code review club
with **SORTEE** ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}).

The club is designed around the barriers it addresses ([Gomes et al. 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="gomes-2022"}): **lack of time and incentive**, **lack of
technical knowledge and unclear workflows**, and **social pressures and the fear
of being judged by peers**.

### Set a clear goal for each session {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Is the focus **general learning and improving readability**, or is it to
**error-check and scrutinise reproducibility**? A clear structure and goal for each session keeps comments and advice focused
on the reason for the review.

Unless the aim is specifically to evaluate different analytical options, it is
better to **leave methodological questions aside**. A session that drifts into
the choice of model is no longer reviewing the code.

### Make it a judgement-free environment {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Volunteers often feel anxious about showing code that may have errors.
**Normalise errors** and stress that perfection is never possible. It also
helps to say that **there is no such thing as bad code**
([Barnes 2010]{.tada-cite data-key="barnes-2010"}), and that there are usually several ways to approach the same
problem.

### Think about group size {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A **smaller group** is a friendlier place to start: people feel more comfortable
speaking up, and it suits peer-to-peer learning and focused review. **Larger
groups** work better for general discussion of themes and tips.

### Decide on credit {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code review outside formal peer review can have a large impact on a project,
from error checking to confirming that the statistical analyses are appropriate.
So what should reviewers get?

- **Acknowledgement via MeRIT** (Method Reporting with Initials for
  Transparency; [Nakagawa et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="nakagawa-2023"}), for example: *"…mixed model with a Gaussian error distribution.
  Code was checked by E.I.C."*
- **Co-authorship**, where the review substantially changed the project and the
  paper, for instance where a reviewer finds a major coding error that, once
  fixed, changes the results and conclusions.

We think credit should match the reviewer's impact on the project ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}).

## A reviewer's script {#review-script}

::: {.tada-wiki}
A sequence for a single review session, built on the four Rs. The full checklist
is at [`templates/code-review-checklist.md`](templates/code-review-checklist.md).
:::

**Before the session (reviewer, 20 minutes)**

1. Download the project into a **new, empty folder**.
2. Open the README. Can you tell what to run, in what order, and what you need
   installed? Note anything you had to guess.
3. Try to run it, in a **fresh session**. Record every error word for word, and stop
   at the first one you cannot resolve in two minutes.

**In the session**

4. **Reported.** Walk the methods section against the code, section by section.
   Flag anything described in the paper you cannot find in the code, and
   anything in the code not described in the paper.
5. **Run.** Go through the errors you hit. Most will be environment or path
   problems, and most are quick to fix.
6. **Reliable.** Pick the two or three steps where a silent error would matter
   most, such as the filtering step, a join or the model specification, and read
   them closely with the author. Ask what each column is.
7. **Reproducible.** Take three numbers from the results section and find them
   in the output.

**Afterwards**

8. Write it up as a short list, ordered by severity, separating **must fix**
   from **would be nice**.
9. Agree how the reviewer will be credited.

::: {.tada-tip}
**Give feedback on the code, not the coder.** "This line reads `mass`, is that
the right column?" is easier to act on than "you used the wrong column". Fear of
being judged is one of the barriers we identified ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}; [Gomes et al. 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="gomes-2022"}), so the way you phrase comments affects whether people keep volunteering.
:::

## Checklist {#review-checklist}

:::: {.tada-checklist-head}
::: {.tada-dog-float}
![](assets/figures/dog-sad.png){.tada-dog-sad alt="A sad cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
![](assets/figures/dog-happy.png){.tada-dog-happy alt="A happy cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
:::

::: {.tada-dog-hint}
Try doing all of these to make the dog happy.
:::
::::

- [ ] **Reported.** The code does what the methods section says it does
- [ ] Software and key packages, with versions, are stated
- [ ] **Run.** The code executes from a fresh download in a fresh session
- [ ] All required libraries are installed and loaded within the code
- [ ] File paths are relative and resolve
- [ ] **Reliable.** Filtering, joins and model specifications have been read closely by someone who knows the data
- [ ] Seeds are set before stochastic steps
- [ ] **Reproducible.** Spot-checked numbers from the results section match the output
- [ ] Mismatches are explained (version, stochasticity, post-processing) and documented
- [ ] Slow or proprietary steps have saved outputs archived
- [ ] The reviewer's contribution is credited (MeRIT, acknowledgement, or authorship)
